{{short description|American scientist}}
'''George Khoury''' (1943 – April 25, 1987) was an American scientist who was chief of the molecular virology laboratory at the [[National Cancer Institute]] from 1980 to his death. He conducted early research with [[enhancer (genetics)|enhancers]] and was elected to membership in the [[National Academy of Sciences]] shortly before his death from [[lymphoma]].

==Biography==
Born in [[Pittsburgh]] to George and Dorothy Khoury, he attended [[William Allen High School]].<ref name="Call">{{cite news|title=Dr. George Khoury, 43, researcher, aide at NIH|url=https://www.mcall.com/1987/04/29/dr-george-khoury-43-researcher-aide-at-nih/|access-date=April 5, 2016|work=[[The Morning Call]]|date=April 29, 1987}}</ref> Khoury graduated from [[Princeton University]] and [[Harvard Medical School]]. At Harvard, he received early research training from [[John Franklin Enders]], and he began to study [[SV40]] with Jan van der Noorda. After a year as a medical intern at [[Massachusetts General Hospital]], Khoury joined NIH as a research associate. He conducted early investigations into transcription patterns in the SV40 genome.<ref name="Cell">{{cite journal|last1=Livingston|first1=David|title=George Khoury (1943–1987)|journal=[[Cell (journal)|Cell]]|date=June 5, 1987|volume=49|issue=5|page=577|url=http://www.cell.com/cell/pdf/0092-8674(87)90529-0.pdf|accessdate=April 5, 2016|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(87)90529-0|pmid=3555839|s2cid=35613732|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In 1980, Khoury was named chief of the Laboratory of Molecular Biology at the National Cancer Institute.<ref name="NYT">{{cite news|title=Dr. George Khoury|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/04/30/obituaries/dr-george-khoury.html|accessdate=April 5, 2016|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=April 30, 1987}}</ref> At NCI, Khoury's lab uncovered the first genetic enhancer while working with SV40. [[Nadia Rosenthal]], one of the researchers in Khoury's lab, later found the first human enhancer.<ref name="Science">{{cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=Ingfei|title=Renaissance woman|journal=Science of Aging Knowledge Environment |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/renaissance-woman|accessdate=April 5, 2016|date=June 20, 2003|volume=2003|issue=24|pages=12nf–12|doi=10.1126/sageke.2003.24.nf12|pmid=12844541|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Khoury played a large part in the establishment of the microbiology department at Princeton University, and he helped to establish a research program for undergraduates that was jointly administered by the NIH and the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]].<ref name=Call/>

Khoury received an [[Arthur S. Flemming Award]] in 1981 in recognition of outstanding service to the U.S. government.<ref name="WP">{{cite news|title=NIH molecular biologist Dr. George Khoury dies|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1987/04/29/nih-molecular-biologist-dr-george-khoury-dies/51cf58aa-3278-45cb-946a-9687db442726/|accessdate=April 5, 2016|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=April 29, 1987}}</ref> He was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1987.<ref name="IRP">{{cite web|title=The National Academy of Sciences and of Engineering|date=7 April 2011 |url=https://irp.nih.gov/about-us/honors/the-national-academy-of-sciences|publisher=[[National Institutes of Health]]|access-date=April 5, 2016}}</ref>

Khoury was treated for lymphoma in the last few years of his life; he went into remission several times.<ref name="Weinberg">{{cite journal |last1=Weinberg |first1=Robert |title=George Khoury (1943-1987) |journal=Nature |date=June 18, 1987 |volume=327 |issue=6123 |page=557 |doi=10.1038/327557a0 |bibcode=1987Natur.327..557W |s2cid=4364339 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/327557a0.pdf}}</ref> He died of the illness shortly after he was elected to the NAS. He was survived by a wife, Marilyn, and two children.<ref name=NYT/> The George Khoury Lecture was established in his memory by NIH.<ref name="Lecture">{{cite web|title=George Khoury Lecture|url=https://oir.nih.gov/wals/named-honorific-lectures/george-khoury-lecture|publisher=[[National Institutes of Health]]|accessdate=April 5, 2016}}</ref> A scholarship in his name, The George Khoury '65 Prize for Academic Excellence, is awarded each year to a senior in the Molecular Biology Department at Princeton University.
